title: Epistaxis
subject: Medicine
summary: Nosebleeds are common and usually benign, but can signal serious bleeding disorders or vascular disease. Assess severity, source, and underlying cause to guide urgent and definitive care.

sections.p: Epistaxis is bleeding from the nasal cavity, identified by visible blood from one or both nostrils. Diagnosis is clinical, based on history and anterior nasal examination.
b: Confirm active bleeding vs. dried blood
Determine laterality and source (anterior vs. posterior)
Assess hemodynamic status (pulse, BP, capillary refill)

sections.p: Severity is staged by volume, duration, and hemodynamic impact. The common three‑tier system is used in low‑resource settings.
Causes are grouped by local, systemic, and iatrogenic factors. In East Africa, local trauma and infectious causes dominate.
b: Local trauma (nose picking, facial injury)
Dry climate / low humidity causing mucosal crusting
Infection: rhinosinusitis, malaria‑related thrombocytopenia
Systemic coagulopathy: vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, HIV‑related thrombocytopenia
Anticoagulant/antiplatelet use (e.g., aspirin, warfarin)
Herbal nasal preparations causing mucosal irritation

sections.p: Patients report sudden blood flow from one or both nostrils, often after a precipitating event. Posterior bleeds may present with blood in the oropharynx and coughing.
b: Bright red blood dripping from nostril(s)
Blood pooling in the nares or posterior pharynx
History of recent nose picking, trauma, or upper‑respiratory infection
Associated symptoms: dizziness, palpitations, shortness of breath if volume is large

t.b: Detect anemia, thrombocytopenia, or leukocytosis; low platelets suggest a systemic bleeding diathesis
Assess extrinsic pathway; prolonged PT indicates vitamin K deficiency or liver disease
Assess intrinsic pathway; prolonged aPTT points to hemophilia or lupus anticoagulant
Locate bleeding source; confirms posterior bleed when anterior packing fails
Identify hemodynamic compromise; hypotension mandates urgent fluid resuscitation

sections.p: Complications arise from uncontrolled bleeding, anemia, or underlying disease.
b: Persistent bleeding >30 minutes despite pressure
Systolic BP <90 mmHg or heart rate >120 bpm
Recurrent severe epistaxis (>3 episodes/year)
Signs of intracranial bleed (headache, vomiting, neurological deficit) after severe posterior bleed

sections.p: Initial steps focus on stabilisation, then local control, and finally treatment of the underlying cause.
b: Place patient upright, lean forward, apply firm pressure to Kiesselbach’s area for 10 minutes
If bleeding continues, use topical vasoconstrictor (e.g., oxymetazoline) – avoid in hypertension
Anterior packing with gauze or commercial tampon if pressure fails
Cauterisation (chemical with silver nitrate or electrical) of identified vessel
Posterior packing or balloon tamponade for posterior bleeds – requires ENT support
Treat systemic causes: vitamin K for deficiency, antiretroviral therapy for HIV‑related thrombocytopenia, stop anticoagulants if safe
Tranexamic acid (IV or topical) can be used when coagulation is impaired – avoid in active thromboembolism

sections.p: After control, address risk factors and arrange follow‑up to prevent recurrence.
b: Educate on gentle nasal hygiene, humidification, and avoiding nose picking
Review and adjust anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy
Screen for anemia or platelet disorders if recurrent
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and manage HIV to reduce coagulopathy

sections.p: Conditions that may mimic epistaxis or coexist.
b: Nasal foreign body causing bleeding
Nasal tumor (e.g., nasopharyngeal carcinoma) presenting with recurrent posterior bleed
Upper airway cough causing blood‑tinged sputum

sections.p: Lab values may be normal early or falsely altered by technical issues.
b: Platelet count can be falsely low if sample is delayed in a hot climate
PT/INR may be normal in early vitamin K deficiency; repeat after 12 hours if suspicion remains

whenToSeekHelp: Bleeding that does not stop after 30 minutes of firm pressure
Signs of shock (BP <90 mmHg, HR >120 bpm, altered mental status)

faq.q: Why is Kiesselbach’s area the most common source?
faq.a: It is a vascular anastomosis on the anterior septum where many small arteries converge, making it vulnerable to trauma and dryness.

faq.q: When should I consider a posterior bleed?
faq.a: If blood is seen in the posterior pharynx, the patient coughs up blood, or anterior packing fails, suspect posterior epistaxis.

faq.q: Can I use nasal decongestant sprays long term to prevent epistaxis?
faq.a: Short‑term use helps control bleeding, but chronic use can cause rebound congestion and mucosal atrophy, increasing bleed risk.

exam: A 12‑year‑old presents with 20 minutes of unilateral bleeding after nose picking – what is your immediate management? — Apply firm pressure to Kiesselbach’s area for 10 minutes, use topical vasoconstrictor, and assess hemodynamics.

A patient on warfarin has a posterior bleed that persists despite anterior packing – what next step? — Arrange posterior packing or balloon tamponade and reverse anticoagulation if INR >3, after weighing thrombotic risk.
How does HIV‑related thrombocytopenia change your approach to epistaxis? — Expect low platelets, obtain CBC, consider tranexamic acid, and coordinate with HIV care for ART optimization.

What clinical feature distinguishes an anterior from a posterior epistaxis? — Posterior bleeds produce blood in the oropharynx and may cause coughing, while anterior bleeds are visible at the nostril.
Why is silver nitrate cautery contraindicated on a septal perforation? — It can enlarge the perforation and cause further bleeding; avoid if perforation is present.

A patient with chronic rhinosinusitis and frequent bleeds is found to have a low vitamin K level – what is the rationale for giving vitamin K? — Vitamin K restores synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X, correcting the coagulopathy that predisposes to bleeding.

Explain why tranexamic acid is useful in epistaxis but should be avoided in a patient with recent deep‑vein thrombosis. — It inhibits fibrinolysis, stabilising clots, but may increase thrombotic risk in patients with active clotting disorders.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt you to order a head CT in a patient with epistaxis? — New onset severe headache, vomiting, or focal neurological deficit suggesting intracranial hemorrhage.
